x-m-el-cul-01.title: Is a credit card really the “golden ratio”?
x-m-el-cul-01.topic: Ratio, symmetry, and patterns in art and daily life
x-m-el-cul-01.goal: Calculate ratios and compare them with a claim, and set your own standard for how much of a difference to allow before using the words “it is the golden ratio.”
x-m-el-cul-01.material: A blog post has this sentence: 'A credit card is a rectangle of 85.6mm by 53.98mm, whose long side to short side ratio is the golden ratio.' The golden ratio is (1 plus the square root of 5) divided by 2, that is, about 1.618. The sizes (long side : short side) of the cases to compare are as follows. A4 paper 297mm : 210mm, a postcard 148mm : 100mm, and a monitor screen with a 16 to 10 ratio, 16 : 10.
x-m-el-cul-01.thinking.0: Evaluate a claim using evidence (calculated ratios)
x-m-el-cul-01.thinking.1: Set and apply a tolerance standard
x-m-el-cul-01.prereq.0: Finding the ratio of two lengths by division (middle school level)
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s1.prompt: You want to evaluate the blog sentence 'A credit card is a golden ratio rectangle.' Divide the long side by the short side and choose the best evaluation.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s1.hint.0: Divide the long side by the short side and put that value next to 1.618.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s1.hint.1: Think separately about whether the two values are “equal” and “how much they differ.”
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s1.o.a: The quotient 1.586 rounds to 1.6, so you can say it is exactly the golden ratio
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s1.r.a: You are using a value rounded to look the same as evidence for “equal.” Check that the conclusion changes depending on how many digits you round to.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s1.o.b: 1.586 and 1.618 are different, so a credit card has nothing to do with the golden ratio at all
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s1.r.b: You are splitting it into only “equal / not at all.” You didn't consider how big the difference is.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s1.explain: 85.6÷53.98 is about 1.586, which differs from the golden ratio 1.618 by about 2%. In a case like this, “close to the golden ratio” is the honest expression, rather than “exactly the golden ratio.”
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s2.prompt: You set the standard: 'If the long side ÷ short side differs from 1.618 by within 3%, it is close to the golden ratio.' Choose all the cases that can be called close. (3% of 1.618 is about 0.049.)
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s2.hint.0: Change each case's ratio to a decimal.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s2.r.a: Check again how you read the difference in the step of finding the ratio and comparing with the standard. Work out whether the difference between this value and 1.618 is inside the allowed range.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s2.r.b: You found the ratio and compared the difference from 1.618 with the allowed range.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s2.r.c: Check whether you worked out yourself if the difference between the postcard's ratio and 1.618 is inside the allowed range. A feeling that they look alike by eye is different from comparing against the standard.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s2.r.d: You changed 16÷10 to a decimal and compared it with the standard.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s2.explain: Only the credit card, 1.586 (about 2.0% difference), and the monitor, 1.6 (about 1.1%), are within 3%. A4 is about 1.414 (about 12.6%) and the postcard is 1.48 (about 8.5%), outside the range.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s3.prompt: The tolerance (here 3%) is a standard I set. Write in one or two sentences why you must set the tolerance before saying “it is the golden ratio,” and what to be careful about when setting the standard.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s3.hint.0: First write in one sentence why a judgment made without a standard is a problem.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine what happens to A4 and the postcard if you set the standard very large (for example, 20%).
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you give as a reason that “exactly the same value” almost never exists in reality?
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write what happens if the standard is too large or too small?
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Can you say how the credit card and the postcard split apart under your standard?
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s3.model.0: Measured values always have error and rulers aren't exact, so exactly equal values almost never exist. So you should first set a tolerance like 1% or 3%, and say it is close if it is within that. If you set the standard too large, almost every rectangle becomes a golden ratio.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s3.model.1: A rectangle that is exactly 1.618 almost never exists in reality, so you have to set a range like within 5%. But if you make the range 10%, the postcard (about 8.5% difference) is included too and the standard becomes too loose.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s1.o.c: The ratio is about 1.586, which is different from 1.618, so 'close' is the accurate word
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s1.r.c: You compared the calculated value with the value in the claim, and you told 'equal' apart from 'close'.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s1.o.d: A ratio measured in mm changes when converted to cm, so the values cannot be compared with each other
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s1.r.d: You think the ratio changes when the unit changes. Check what happens to a ratio of two lengths measured in the same unit when the unit is converted.
x-m-el-cul-01.s.s2.hint.1: Subtract 0.049 from 1.618 and add 0.049 to it to find the allowed interval yourself, then check whether each ratio falls inside it.

x-m-el-cul-02.title: Finding the wrong line in a symmetry table
x-m-el-cul-02.topic: Ratio, symmetry, and patterns in art and daily life
x-m-el-cul-02.goal: Find and correct the error in a solution that sums up the number of lines of symmetry, and pick out yourself which shapes have exactly 2 lines of symmetry.
x-m-el-cul-02.material: Symmetry is often used in traditional patterns and architectural design. A student made a table summing up the symmetry of shapes. A line-symmetric figure has a line of symmetry, a line along which the figure overlaps exactly when folded, and a point-symmetric figure is a figure that overlaps its original when turned half a turn (180°) around some point. One of the lines in the table has an error.
x-m-el-cul-02.thinking.0: Find where the error in the solution is
x-m-el-cul-02.thinking.1: Fix the error and explain how to check it
x-m-el-cul-02.thinking.2: Pick out shapes that meet the condition
x-m-el-cul-02.prereq.0: The meaning of line-symmetric figures (they overlap when folded along some line) and point-symmetric figures (they overlap when turned 180° around a point)
x-m-el-cul-02.prereq.1: Properties of rectangles, rhombuses, and parallelograms
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in the table with wrong content.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine folding the shape in each line with paper and count its lines of symmetry one by one.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s1.hint.1: Don't suspect just one line because it has many lines of symmetry; check for each line whether the shape really overlaps when folded.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s1.line.0: Equilateral triangle: it has 3 lines of symmetry and is not a point-symmetric figure.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s1.line.1: Square: it has 4 lines of symmetry and is a point-symmetric figure.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s1.line.2: Rectangle (not a square): the 2 lines in the length and width directions and the two diagonals, 4 in all, are lines of symmetry, and it is a point-symmetric figure.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s1.line.3: Parallelogram (not a rectangle or rhombus): it has no lines of symmetry, and is a point-symmetric figure.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s1.line.4: Regular pentagon: it has 5 lines of symmetry and is not a point-symmetric figure.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. If you fold a rectangle that is not a square along a diagonal, the long side goes over the short side and the vertices don't overlap. It has only 2 lines of symmetry, folding in half in the length and width directions. The part saying it is point-symmetric is right.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s2.prompt: Correct what line 3 says, and write how to check that a diagonal is not a line of symmetry in that shape.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s2.hint.0: Think about where the long side and short side go when you fold a rectangular piece of paper along a diagonal.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s2.hint.1: Compare folding along a diagonal with the case of a square.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say the corrected number is 2 and which direction the lines go?
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain, using side lengths or vertices, why folding along the diagonal doesn't overlap?
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you tell this apart from why the diagonals of a square are lines of symmetry?
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s2.model.0: A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry. If you fold it along a diagonal, the long side lies on the short side, so the vertices don't overlap.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s2.model.1: There are only two lines of symmetry, folding in half lengthwise and widthwise. If you fold along a diagonal, one triangle doesn't lie on top of the other. It is because the side lengths are different.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s3.prompt: Choose all the shapes below that have exactly 2 lines of symmetry.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s3.hint.0: Draw all the lines along which each shape overlaps when folded.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s3.hint.1: Compare where the lines of symmetry pass in a rectangle and in a rhombus.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s3.r.a: This is the result of counting lines of symmetry by folding.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s3.r.b: Fold again to count how many lines of symmetry this shape has. Think only of the line through the apex angle.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s3.r.c: You may have mixed up the property of being point-symmetric with the property of being line-symmetric. Check separately by folding whether it overlaps.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s3.r.d: This is a shape whose two diagonals are lines of symmetry. It is the result of counting while telling point symmetry and line symmetry apart.
x-m-el-cul-02.s.s3.explain: A rectangle has 2, in the length and width directions, and a rhombus has 2, its two diagonals. An isosceles triangle has 1 and a parallelogram has 0.

x-m-el-cul-03.title: Designing a 100-block sidewalk pattern
x-m-el-cul-03.topic: Ratio, symmetry, and patterns in art and daily life
x-m-el-cul-03.goal: Design several repeating patterns that satisfy a fixed ratio and length conditions all at once, and explain why the possible periods have a common rule.
x-m-el-cul-03.material: On a row of 100 sidewalk blocks, red blocks and blue blocks are laid in turn. The pattern takes 'r red blocks followed by (p−r) blue blocks' as one group and repeats this group. The conditions are as follows. (1) p is a natural number from 2 to 50, and r is a natural number from 1 up to less than p. (2) The last group is not cut off, and the 100 blocks end exactly. (3) There are exactly 40 red blocks (40% of the total).
x-m-el-cul-03.thinking.1: Find what the solutions have in common
x-m-el-cul-03.thinking.2: Connect the ratio with the natural number conditions
x-m-el-cul-03.prereq.0: Ratio (part of the whole) and multiplication and division of natural numbers
x-m-el-cul-03.prereq.1: The meaning of divisors and multiples
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s0.hint.0: First write how many groups there are (100÷p), then multiply by how many red blocks are in each group.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s0.explain: Since the group repeats in the same form, if red blocks are 40% of the whole, red blocks must be 40% in one group too. This is the condition between r and p.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.prompt: Make three different patterns that satisfy all the conditions. p is the number of blocks in one group, and r is the number of red blocks in one group.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.hint.0: First, write candidates for what number p must be so that 100 blocks end exactly with groups of p blocks.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.hint.1: For each candidate p, find the number of groups, and find what r must be for there to be 40 red blocks.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.var.p: Number of blocks in one group, p
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.var.r: Number of red blocks in one group, r
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.ok.c1: p and r are natural numbers.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.fail.c1: p and r must be natural numbers.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.ok.c2: The ranges of p and r are right.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.fail.c2: p must be 2 to 50, and r must be at least 1 and less than p.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.ok.c3: The 100 blocks end exactly with groups.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.fail.c3: The group gets cut off. The 100 blocks must divide evenly into groups of p blocks.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.fail.c4: There are not 40 red blocks. Check by multiplying the number of groups by r.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.explain: (p, r) = (5, 2), (10, 4), (20, 8), (25, 10), (50, 20) all satisfy the conditions. For example, if p=20 and r=8, there are 5 groups and the red blocks are 8×5=40.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.because.prompt: The p values you found are all multiples of what number? Explain in one or two sentences why this happens.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.because.hint.0: Change the expression r × (number of groups) = 40 into an expression for r.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.because.selfAssess.0: Is your reason connected to the ratio that 'red blocks are 2/5 of the whole'?
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain using a case like 'p=3, r=1.2' where r does not become a natural number?
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.because.model.0: Red blocks are 40% of the whole, that is 2/5, so red blocks must be 2/5 in one group too. For r to be a natural number, p must be a multiple of 5.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.because.model.1: If r×(100÷p)=40, then r=0.4×p. For 0.4×p to be a natural number, p must be a multiple of 5.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s0.prompt: Let's sort it out first. For exactly 40 of the 100 cells to be red, what condition must hold for one bundle (p cells)? (This is the case where the 100 cells end exactly at the end of a bundle.)
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s0.hint.1: Write an equation so that the total number of red cells is 40, then turn that equation into a relationship between r and p.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s0.o.a: The fraction of red cells in one bundle, r÷p, must be 40%
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s0.r.a: Because the bundle repeats in the same pattern, you saw that the rate in one bundle equals the rate in the whole.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s0.o.b: The ratio of red to blue in one bundle, r : (p−r), must be 40 : 100
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s0.r.b: You mixed up a ratio comparing red with blue and the share of red out of the whole. The 40% is the share of red cells out of all 100 cells.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s0.o.c: The number of bundles, 100÷p, must equal the number of red cells in one bundle, r
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s0.r.c: You mixed up the number of bundles and the number of red cells. Think about how many red cells there are in each bundle.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s0.o.d: The number of red cells in one bundle, r, must be 40
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s0.r.d: You treated the number of red cells in one bundle as the same as the total number of red cells. Think about how many times the bundle repeats.
x-m-el-cul-03.s.s1.because.hint.1: Pick a few divisors of 100, such as p=4 or p=20, calculate r, and separate the cases where r is a natural number from those where it is not.

x-m-el-cul-04.title: Did the campaign reduce garbage?
x-m-el-cul-04.goal: To judge a causal claim from the data 'garbage went down after the campaign,' sort out what information is needed, and write concretely how the conclusion changes depending on the result.
x-m-el-cul-04.material: A district office ran a recycling campaign in 2024. According to the district office's data, the monthly average household garbage went from 1,200 tons in 2023, the year before the campaign, to 1,080 tons in 2025, a 10% decrease (10% of 1,200 is 120). The district office's website says, 'The recycling campaign reduced garbage by 10%.'
x-m-el-cul-04.thinking.0: Judge the link between a claim and the information needed
x-m-el-cul-04.thinking.1: Think about comparison groups and background factors
x-m-el-cul-04.prereq.0: The meaning of rate of increase and rate of decrease
x-m-el-cul-04.prereq.1: Reading changes over time from a graph or table
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.prompt: To evaluate the statement 'the campaign is the cause,' which of the following information is needed? Choose all that are needed.
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.hint.0: Even if the '10% decrease' is true, that the reason is the campaign has to be checked separately. Write what reasons other than the campaign there could be for the decrease.
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.hint.1: Judge whether each choice helps rule out one reason other than the campaign.
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.o.a: The number of residents who took part in the campaign petition
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.r.a: The number of participants can tell you how the campaign worked. But it can't separate whether the cause of the decrease was the campaign or another reason.
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.o.b: The trend in garbage output over the several years before the campaign
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.r.b: This is the idea of checking whether the flow was already decreasing regardless of the campaign.
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.o.c: The month with the most garbage in 2025
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.r.c: The maximum of one month is not directly used for judging whether the 10% decrease is because of the campaign.
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.o.d: The change over the same period in a similar district that did not run the campaign
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.r.d: This is the idea of checking by comparison whether there was a factor other than the campaign.
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.o.e: The change in the district's population or number of households over the same period
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.r.e: This is the idea of checking whether the total decreasing was because the number of people changed.
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.explain: To talk about a cause, you need (1) the trend before the campaign, (2) a comparison group that did not run the campaign, and (3) background changes like population. The number of petition signers and the month with the maximum aren't directly used to separate out the cause of the 10% decrease.
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s1.acc.0: The trend and the comparison district are the key information. Looking at the population change too makes it more certain.
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s2.prompt: Choose one of the needed pieces of information, and write what result of it would be evidence for the side 'the campaign had an effect' and what result would be evidence for the side 'it's hard to say there was an effect.'
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s2.hint.0: Think separately about when the information you chose is 'large' and when it is 'small.'
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s2.hint.1: Judge in each case whether the explanation 'because of the campaign' is convincing.
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write both of the opposite results for the information you chose?
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say 'so I judge this' for each result?
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is it clear which you chose, a comparison group or a background factor?
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s2.model.0: If we look at the change in a comparison district over the same period: if the comparison district stayed almost the same and only our district dropped 10%, that is evidence of a campaign effect, and if the comparison district also dropped about 10%, it is hard to say it was because of the campaign.
x-m-el-cul-04.s.s2.model.1: If we look at the trend over the several years before the campaign: if it had been almost constant and dropped only after the campaign, we can say there was an effect, and if it was already a trend of dropping 10% every year, it is hard to say it was the campaign's effect.

x-m-el-cul-05.title: The story of the “average of 400만 원” village
x-m-el-cul-05.goal: Revise your judgment each time the data are revealed step by step, and say what you can't know from the mean alone.
x-m-el-cul-05.material: A village notice says, 'The average monthly income of our village's 10 households is 400만 원.' You want to judge the village after reading this notice.
x-m-el-cul-05.thinking.0: Revise your judgment to fit new information
x-m-el-cul-05.thinking.1: Compare the mean and the median
x-m-el-cul-05.thinking.2: Rewrite into a sentence that doesn't cause misunderstanding
x-m-el-cul-05.prereq.0: The meaning of the mean and the median (the middle value when put in order of size)
x-m-el-cul-05.prereq.1: Reading the distribution of data in a table
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose the best judgment and then revise it.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.hint.0: Each time the revealed information grows, separate 'what you can say for sure with this information' from 'what you can't say yet.'
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.hint.1: Think of another income distribution that gives a mean of 400.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.0.info: The only information revealed is 'the average monthly income of the 10 households is 400만 원.'
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: From this information alone, can you say about how many households have a monthly income of 400만 원 or more?
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.0.after: The mean is the sum of all values divided by the number of households, so with the same mean, both a village where income is spread evenly and a village where one household is very high are possible.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Most (8 or more households) will be at 400만 원 or more
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You think that if the mean is 400, most are near 400. Make one different data set whose mean is 400.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Exactly 5 households will be at 400만 원 or more
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You are mistaking the mean for the 'middle.' Are the mean and the middle value always the same?
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: You can't know how many households from the mean alone
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You pointed out that the mean doesn't tell you the distribution of the values.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.1.info: Next, the median is revealed. The median is the middle value when incomes are put in order from smallest, and for 10 households it is the average of the 5th and 6th incomes. This village's median is 250만 원.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: Looking at the mean of 400만 원 and the median of 250만 원 together, what is the greatest number of households with a monthly income of 400만 원 or more?
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.1.after: If the median is 250, the incomes of the 5 households on the smaller side are all 250 or less, so at most 5 households are at 400만 원 or more. If the mean is much greater than the median, it is likely that a few high values pulled the mean up.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You read the median 250 as meaning the 5 households on the smaller side are at 250 or less.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You may have missed the limit the median of 250 places on the number of upper households. If 7 households are at 400 or more, what would the 5th income have to be?
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You did not take the median into account. Think about what the middle value would be if 9 households were at 400 or more.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.2.info: Finally, the monthly incomes of the 10 households are revealed from smallest (in 만 원). 200, 200, 220, 240, 250, 250, 260, 280, 300, 1800.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which is the best notice to announce the income of a 'typical' household in this village?
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.2.after: Nine households are at 200 to 300만 원 and one household is at 1,800만 원, which makes the mean 400. With a distribution like this, you need to give the median or the distribution along with the mean to avoid misunderstanding.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Write in big letters at the top of the notice that, since the mean is 400, most residents earn about 400만 원 a month
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This judgment read the mean only as the 'typical' value. Compare it with the actual households' incomes.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Write that, since the mean is 400, this village's household incomes are evenly clustered
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You drew the conclusion that it is even from the fact that the mean is the same. Look at the gap between the largest value and the rest.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Write that one household is high, which raised the mean, and most are at 200 to 300만 원
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You looked at the mean and the distribution together and told the income range of most households.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s1.reflect: The one number, the mean of 400, was read differently at each step. Look back at how you changed your earlier judgment when new information came in, and what was risky about a notice that used only the mean.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite the notice's 'The average monthly income is 400만 원' so it doesn't cause misunderstanding. Use two or more numbers.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s2.hint.0: Instead of the mean 400, what number tells you the income of the 'middle household'?
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s2.hint.1: Put the reason in one sentence too, so the neighbors reading the notice don't misunderstand.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you use the mean and the median together and explain the reason for the difference between them (one very high household)?
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Can the reader tell about how much a 'typical household' probably earns?
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s2.model.0: The mean is 400만 원, but one household earns 1,800만 원, which raised the mean, and the median is 250만 원, and most households earn 300만 원 or less.
x-m-el-cul-05.s.s2.model.1: The household in the middle of the incomes earns 250만 원 (the median), and the mean of 400만 원 is a value raised by one very high household.

x-m-el-cul-06.title: The mean is under the standard, but some places are over it
x-m-el-cul-06.goal: Make your own counterexample data to the claim 'the mean is under the standard, so everywhere is safe,' and explain what the mean hides.
x-m-el-cul-06.material: A city's environment department announced, 'Today the mean of the fine dust (PM2.5) at 3 measuring stations is 30㎍/㎥ (micrograms per cubic meter), which is under the standard value 35, so all areas are safe.' In this task, the standard value is set at 35, and each station's value is an integer from 10 to 60.
x-m-el-cul-06.thinking.2: Find several examples that meet the conditions
x-m-el-cul-06.prereq.0: Calculating the mean of three numbers
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s0.prompt: To show the announcement can be wrong, what data should you make?
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s0.hint.0: Split the announcement's claim into the 'mean 30' part and the 'all safe' part.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s0.hint.1: Think about which part to leave as it is and which part to break to make a counterexample.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s0.o.a: Data in which all three stations' values are exactly 30, so you can confirm the mean is 30
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s0.r.a: This shows a case where the announcement is right. What data do you need to test the claim that the announcement can be wrong?
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s0.o.b: Data where the mean goes over 35, so it is immediately clear the announcement was wrong
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s0.r.b: The mean in the announcement is 30, so changing the mean tests a different claim.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s0.o.c: Data where the mean is 30 but some station is over the standard 35
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s0.r.c: You aimed for data that shows the second of the announcement's two parts (mean 30, all safe) can be wrong.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s0.o.d: Taking one station out by itself and making data where its value is 30
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s0.r.d: If there is only one station, the mean and the individual value are the same, so you can't show the difference between them.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s0.explain: The announcement's claim is 'the mean is under the standard, so all are safe.' If you keep the mean at 30 and make data where some station is over the standard, you can show this reasoning is not always right.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.prompt: You want to show the announcement can be wrong. Make three different data sets where the three stations' values (a, b, c) have a mean of 30 but at least one is over the standard value 35. (Data that differ only in the order of the values count as the same data.)
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.hint.0: First decide what the sum of the three values must be for the mean to be 30.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.hint.1: Choose one value greater than 35, then adjust so the other two values' sum works out.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.fail.c1: Please enter the values as integers.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.fail.c3: The mean of the three values is not 30. Think about what the sum should be.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.ok.c4: There is a station over the standard value 35.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.fail.c4: There is no station over the standard value 35.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.explain: (40, 40, 10), (50, 30, 10), (60, 20, 10), (45, 30, 15): the sum is 90 and one value is over 35, and that works. Even if the mean 30 is under the standard, individual stations can be over the standard.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.because.prompt: Using this data, explain why the environment department's statement 'the mean is under the standard, so all areas are safe' can be wrong.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.because.hint.0: Write the mean and the largest value side by side in the data you made.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.because.hint.1: Say how a high value looks in the mean when it is combined with low values.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.because.selfAssess.0: Did you explain using the concrete numbers you made?
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the mean mixes high values and low values together?
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.because.selfAssess.2: Did you say what you need to look at to confirm that 'all are safe'?
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.because.model.0: Even if the mean is 30, if one site is 40, that site is over the standard 35. The mean mixes high places and low places together, so you can't see the condition of individual sites.
x-m-el-cul-06.s.s1.because.model.1: Even if the mean is under the standard, some sites can be over it. It is because low values offset high values. To know whether all areas are safe, you have to look at each station's value separately.

x-m-el-cul-07.title: The bar is 3 times as tall, but sales differ by 2%?
x-m-el-cul-07.goal: Find and fix the error in a solution that misread a bar graph whose vertical axis doesn't start at 0, and judge when the starting value of an axis is acceptable.
x-m-el-cul-07.material: A smartphone company's ad material has a bar graph. The vertical axis starts at 990 and one grid mark means 10만 units. Model A's bar is 3 grid marks high and Model B's bar is 1 grid mark high. The table lists the actual sales. A student wrote a solution reading the graph.
x-m-el-cul-07.thinking.0: Find the error in reading a graph
x-m-el-cul-07.thinking.1: Explain the cause of the misunderstanding
x-m-el-cul-07.thinking.2: Judge when a starting value of an axis is allowed
x-m-el-cul-07.prereq.0: Reading grid marks on a bar graph
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the wrong line in the student's solution.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s1.hint.0: Separate whether each line talks about the look of the graph or about the actual values.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think about where the vertical axis would have to start for the bar heights to have the same ratio as the actual values.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s1.line.0: The vertical axis starts at 990, and one grid mark means 10만 units.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s1.line.1: Bar A is drawn 3 grid marks high and bar B is drawn 1 grid mark high.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s1.line.2: The bar heights are 3 : 1, so A's sales are 3 times B's.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s1.line.3: The actual sales listed in the table are 1,020만 units for A and 1,000만 units for B.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s1.line.4: So A sold about 2% more than B.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The bar heights are lengths measured from 990, not from 0, so the height ratio 3 : 1 is not the ratio of sales. The ratio of actual sales is 1,020÷1,000=1.02 times.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s2.prompt: Correct line 3, and write why this graph is misleading and how it should be drawn to reduce the misunderstanding.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s2.hint.0: Using the fact that the bar heights are lengths measured from 990, think about what would happen if you measured the two bars' actual lengths from 0.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s2.hint.1: Write at least one concrete way to fix it.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the ratio of the bar heights and the ratio of the actual values as different things?
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write a concrete way to fix it (start from 0, write the actual values, show a break mark, etc.)?
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s2.model.0: The vertical axis starts at 990, not 0, so the difference looks big. The actual values are 1,020만 and 1,000만, so the difference is about 2%. If the vertical axis starts at 0, the two bars become almost the same length.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s2.model.1: It looks like 3 times because the bottom of the axis was cut off. The real ratio is about 1.02 times, so you should draw it from 0 or write the actual values above the bars.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s3.prompt: When can a graph whose vertical axis doesn't start at 0 be accepted as relatively less misleading?
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s3.hint.0: For each choice, write what part of the graph (length, position, area) you read the value from.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s3.hint.1: Think about why it is important to state the starting value clearly on the grid marks.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s3.o.a: A bar graph comparing the sizes of two values by bar length
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s3.r.a: You read a bar as having a length proportional to the value, so if the starting point is not 0, the ratio is distorted.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s3.o.b: A line graph that looks at the shape of change (with the starting value shown)
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s3.r.b: This is a graph read by the position of points and slope, and you considered that the starting value was stated.
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s3.o.c: A pie chart that shows at a glance the ratio of each part of the whole
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s3.r.c: You may have missed that a pie chart has no scale axis. First think about where the question uses the 'starting value of the axis.'
x-m-el-cul-07.s.s3.explain: A line graph is read for the shape of change in values, so if the starting value of the axis is clearly stated, it can sometimes start at a value other than 0. A bar graph must start at 0 because length means size. In either case, you must not hide the starting value.

x-m-el-cul-08.title: The graph that says “temperatures are going down”
x-m-el-cul-08.goal: Know that the conclusion can change depending on the period you look at in the data, and revise your judgment each time information is added.
x-m-el-cul-08.material: The title of a graph on a city hall website is 'Our city's temperature keeps going down.' The graph shows the annual average temperature (℃).
x-m-el-cul-08.thinking.0: Don't declare a long-term trend from short-term data
x-m-el-cul-08.thinking.1: Revise a judgment using additional data
x-m-el-cul-08.thinking.2: Choose a fair way to decide the starting year
x-m-el-cul-08.prereq.0: Reading increase and decrease on a line graph
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose the best judgment and then revise it.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, first write how long the period you know about is.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart whether new data contradicts the earlier data or shows a different period.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: From this graph alone, is it okay to say 'this city's temperature has a trend of continuing to go down'?
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.0.after: It's true that it dropped over 4 years, but it is too early to generalize from 4 values to 'a trend of continuing to go down.'
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It went down 4 years in a row, so it's okay to say that
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You read the shape connected by 4 points directly as a long-term trend. Think about what longer-period data for the same city might look like.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Four years is short, so it's too early to say 'a trend of going down'
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You were careful about generalizing because there are only 4 values.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.0.o.c: There are only 4 data points, so you can't say any facts from this graph
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You are denying even the fact that it dropped over 4 years. Tell apart what you can say from what you can't.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.1.ask: Looking at the two data sets together, what is the best judgment?
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.1.after: The two data sets do not contradict each other. They just show different periods. Even within a long-term rise, there can be a few years of decline.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The more recent data, 4 years in a row of decline, should be seen as the real trend now
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You thought the recent data should be trusted more. Check whether you told apart short-period fluctuation from the flow of a long period.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The two data sets say different things, so you can't trust either
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You read data showing different periods as a contradiction. Work out whether both data sets can be true.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Over the long period it is rising, and the recent decline could be a short ups-and-downs
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You accepted both data sets as true and explained it by the difference in the length of the periods.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.2.info: 2018 was 12.8℃ and 2019 was 13.0℃. The website graph is drawn starting from 2020 (13.6℃), and 2020 was the highest year of that period.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is a fair way to decide the starting year of a graph?
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.2.after: With the same data, depending on the starting year, both rising and falling shapes are possible. It is fair to set the standard in advance and also show other periods.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.reflect: How was your judgment different when you looked only at the first graph and after you saw the long-term data? Think about why you should first ask 'which period' you are looking at when you look at a graph.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s2.prompt: Write one sentence about this city's temperature that doesn't cause misunderstanding. Include both the recent change and the flow over a long period.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s2.hint.0: Put the last 4 years and the 10-year averages over 30 years side by side and write how each one changed.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s2.hint.1: Try the sentence frame 'Recently ~, but over a long period ~.'
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you tell apart the change over the last few years and the change over a long period?
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you avoid definite words like 'keeps' and 'always'?
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s2.model.0: The last 4 years went down, but in 10-year units it kept rising, so you can say the long-term trend is upward.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s2.model.1: The decline since 2020 may be a short-term fluctuation, and the 10-year averages over 30 years rose, so the long-term rising trend is more trustworthy.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.1.info: Mean temperatures for each 10-year period in the same city: 12.4℃ for 1994–2003, 12.9℃ for 2004–2013, 13.1℃ for 2014–2023.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Decide the criterion before looking, and also show other periods
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You decided the criterion in advance so that choosing a period would not decide the conclusion, and you gave information that can be compared.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.2.o.b: You should start drawing from the year with the highest value, because that shows the change best
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The idea is to pick a starting point where the change shows up well. Consider that the starting point can decide the conclusion.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Draw it with several starting years and pick the shape that stands out most
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a way of choosing the starting point that fits the conclusion you want to show. This way you can make the opposite impression from the same data.
x-m-el-cul-08.s.s2.model.2: It dropped recently, but over a long period it rose. A drop over a few years after 2020 alone cannot describe the overall trend.

x-m-el-cul-09.title: Making a one-measure rhythm yourself
x-m-el-cul-09.goal: Make several rhythms yourself that meet the condition on the sum of beats, and explain why some notes have limits on how many you can use.
x-m-el-cul-09.material: A measure in 4/4 time has 4 beats. A quarter note takes 1 beat, an eighth note takes 0.5 beat, and a half note takes 2 beats. You want to make a rhythm that fills one measure with exactly 4 beats using only notes, with no rests. So it isn't monotonous, use at least 1 quarter note and at least 2 eighth notes, and use at least 4 notes in all.
x-m-el-cul-09.thinking.1: Think about a way to find them without missing any
x-m-el-cul-09.thinking.2: Connect sums of fractions and decimals with natural number conditions
x-m-el-cul-09.prereq.1: The note lengths are explained in the material
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s0.prompt: You want to find, without missing any, the rhythms that fill one measure with 4 beats. What is the best method?
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s0.hint.0: Start by working out the greatest number of half notes that can fit.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s0.hint.1: Fix one case, then investigate all the possible combinations in that case to the end.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s0.o.a: Pick notes as they come to mind, add the beats, and collect the ones that make 4 beats
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s0.r.a: You can find some, but you can't know whether you found them all.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s0.o.d: Fix the number of quarter notes and stop when one case comes up
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s0.r.d: If you find one and stop, you can't know whether there are more solutions.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s0.explain: If you fix the count of one kind of note as 0, 1, 2 in turn and investigate the rest in each case, you can check that you found them all.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.prompt: Make three different rhythms that meet the conditions. a is the number of quarter notes, b is the number of eighth notes, and c is the number of half notes.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.hint.0: Fix the number of half notes c as 0 or 1, and find ways to fill the remaining beats with quarter notes and eighth notes.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.hint.1: After you find one, change it while keeping the number of beats, such as reducing the eighth notes by 2 and increasing the quarter notes by 1.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.ok.c1: The counts are integers that are 0 or more.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.fail.c1: The note counts must be integers that are 0 or more.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.ok.c2: At least 1 quarter note and at least 2 eighth notes.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.fail.c2: There must be at least 1 quarter note and at least 2 eighth notes.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.fail.c3: The sum of beats is not 4. Multiply each note by its number of beats and add.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.fail.c4: You must use at least 4 notes in all.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.explain: (a, b, c) = (3, 2, 0), (2, 4, 0), (1, 6, 0), (1, 2, 1) are all four that meet every condition. For example, (1, 2, 1) is 1 + 2×0.5 + 2 = 4 beats.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.because.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences why you can't make a rhythm with an odd number of eighth notes.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.because.hint.0: Find how many beats the notes take up when there is 1 eighth note or 3.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.because.hint.1: First work out whether the beats taken by the other notes are a whole number.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.because.selfAssess.0: Did you use the fact that the beats of the other notes are natural numbers?
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say how many eighth notes have to come together to make a whole number of beats?
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.because.model.0: Quarter notes and half notes take a whole number of beats, so the beats made by the remaining eighth notes must also be a whole number. Two eighth notes make 1 beat, so the eighth notes must be an even number.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.because.model.1: One eighth note is 0.5 beat, so with an odd number the sum of beats has .5 left over and can't make 4 beats. So the number is even.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s0.o.b: Fix the number of half notes, and for each case check every possible combination of quarter and eighth notes
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s0.r.b: This is a method of fixing the count of one kind in order and investigating each case all the way through so as not to miss any.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s0.o.c: Fix the number of half notes, and for each case find just one combination of quarter and eighth notes, then move on to the next case
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s0.r.c: Splitting into cases is good, but finding only one within each case misses other solutions in the same case.
x-m-el-cul-09.s.s1.because.model.2: Two eighth notes together make one beat, so if there is an odd number of them, half a beat is left over and you cannot fill 4 beats, a whole number of beats.

x-m-el-cul-10.title: Raised and lowered, but not the original price?
x-m-el-cul-10.topic: Raising then lowering by a percentage
x-m-el-cul-10.goal: Make your own pairs where raising by a percent and then lowering returns to the original value, and explain why the percent raised and the percent lowered are not the same.
x-m-el-cul-10.material: A shop advertises that it first raised an item's price by p% and then immediately lowered it by q%, and it became the same as the original price. p and q are both integers that are at least 1, and p is at most 1000. You lower q% from the raised price.
x-m-el-cul-10.thinking.0: Make pairs yourself that meet the conditions
x-m-el-cul-10.thinking.1: Understand that the base for a percent changes
x-m-el-cul-10.thinking.2: Find a rule from a pattern
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s0.prompt: If an item priced at 100원 is raised by 20% and then immediately lowered by 20%, what happens?
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s0.hint.0: First find the price after the raise, then find 20% of that price.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s0.hint.1: Write what price the percent for the lowering is a rate of.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s0.o.a: No. 20% of 120원 is 24원, so it becomes 96원
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s0.r.a: You calculated using the price after the raise as the base for the lowering.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s0.o.b: Yes. It was raised 20% and lowered 20%, so it's the same as the original price
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s0.r.b: You thought that if the raised and lowered percents are the same, it goes back to the original. Check what the second percent is a rate of.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s0.o.c: Yes. Lowering 20원, which is 20% of 100원, from the raised 120원 gives 100원
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s0.r.c: You used the original price (100원) as the base for the percent when lowering. Check what the base is when lowering from the raised price.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s0.explain: The raised price 120원 becomes the base for the lowering, so 24원, which is 20% of 120원, comes off and it becomes 96원. It doesn't return to the original price of 100원.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s1.prompt: Make three different pairs (p, q) that make the advertisement true. (Pairs with the same p are the same pair.)
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s1.hint.0: Set the price at 100원, find the value after raising by p%, and find what q must be so that lowering q% from that value gives 100원.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s1.hint.1: Choose a few p and find q, but you can only use as a pair a p for which q is an integer.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s1.ok.c1: p and q are integers that are at least 1.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s1.fail.c1: p and q must be integers that are at least 1.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s1.ok.c3: It returns to the original price.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s1.fail.c3: It does not become the original price. Set the original price as 100원 and find the value after raising and lowering.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s1.explain: (p, q) = (25, 20), (100, 50), (150, 60), (300, 75), (400, 80), (900, 90) and so on. For example, raising 100원 by 25% gives 125원, and 20% of 125원 is 25원, so lowering 20% gives 100원.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s1.because.prompt: Why is the percent lowered q always smaller than the percent raised p for the price to return to the original? Give one example with numbers and explain in one or two sentences.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s1.because.hint.0: Calculate directly in two steps the price after raising and then lowering from a price of 100원.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s1.because.hint.1: Write what price the percent for lowering is a rate of.
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s1.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say that the base for the percent when lowering is the raised price, not the original price?
x-m-el-cul-10.s.s1.because.selfAssess.1: Did you use the fact that the amount to be given back is the same?
